cl_gen_most_users_not_addicted.q: Do most people who try drugs get addicted?
cl_gen_most_users_not_addicted.short: Mostly not, except tobacco. In a big US survey, about 9 in 100 people who'd tried cannabis were expected to become dependent at some point. Cocaine 21, alcohol 23, tobacco 68.
cl_gen_most_users_not_addicted.but: It's people's own memories, in one US survey from 2001 to 2005. People in prison, or who had died, weren't asked, so the real figures may be higher.
how: Dependence meant at least 3 of 7 signs in the same year, like needing more for the same effect, withdrawal, or not managing to stop. It came from people's answers, not tests.
For cannabis and cocaine it often came early: half of those who became dependent did so within about 4 to 5 years of first use. For alcohol it took 13 years, for tobacco 27.
People with depression, anxiety or another dependence became dependent more often. That's a link, not proof of a cause.

Drug researcher Carl Hart says most people who use drugs never get addicted. His opinion pieces give no data. The survey fits that for cannabis, cocaine and alcohol, not tobacco. It has no figures for heroin or meth.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had ever tried each one, how many were expected to become dependent at some point?
freq.note: US survey, 2001 to 2005, from the ages people remembered: projections over a lifetime, with no margin of error given. Tobacco 67.5, rounded.

cl_gen_most_users_not_addicted.rate: One large US survey, done carefully, but built on memories, sometimes decades old. The lifetime figures are forecasts, the tobacco one most of all.

cl_opi_vietnam_veterans.q: Did the soldiers addicted to heroin in Vietnam stay addicted?
cl_opi_vietnam_veterans.short: Mostly not. Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home, and 12 in 100 within 3 years.
cl_opi_vietnam_veterans.but: Vietnam was unusual: heroin was cheap, pure and everywhere. The lead researcher says few of these young men would have become addicted at home.
how: In Vietnam in 1970–71, almost half of US Army enlisted men tried narcotics, mostly heroin or opium. 20 in 100 said they'd been addicted there.
Back home, many used again without getting addicted again. Even among men who used heroin often, only about half got addicted again.
Treatment wasn't the reason, the lead researcher says. Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home. Those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.
These are the men's own reports, checked against military records and urine tests. The 3-year figures come from the lead researcher's later lecture, whose text and graphs don't always match.

freq.title: Out of every 100 men addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, how many were addicted again back home?
freq.note: US Army enlisted men who left Vietnam in September 1971, in the lead researcher's later account. Addiction was self-reported, checked against records and urine tests.

cl_opi_vietnam_veterans.rate: One well-run study: nearly every man chosen was interviewed, and answers were checked. But it's one war, in unusual conditions. The 3-year figures come from the lead researcher's later lecture.

cl_gen_remission.q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?
cl_gen_remission.short: Many do. In US surveys, about 8 in 10 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. Treatment was uncommon.
cl_gen_remission.but: That's not the same as quitting. And only alcohol studies counted who got better without treatment.
how: In three US surveys from 1990 to 2003, 76 to 83 in 100 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. They could still use drugs, or relapse later.

Counted one drug at a time, half of people dependent on cocaine had recovered within about 4 years of becoming dependent, cannabis 6, alcohol 16 and cigarettes 30. Some stayed dependent for decades. Heroin wasn't in these figures.
Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years. Few entered drug treatment back home.

In 21 long studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen. For alcohol, counts of recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100. That's mostly because studies count different groups.

freq.what: people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year
freq.note: US national survey, 2001 to 2002, by one researcher's calculation from its published figures (76 and 83 in two other US surveys). No longer counting as dependent is not the same as quitting.

cl_gen_remission.rate: Big US surveys and long studies agree that many people recover. But most figures come second-hand, through reviews. And for drugs other than alcohol, nobody here counted who recovered without treatment.

general.statement: Most people who try cocaine become dependent on it.
general.why: In a big US survey, about 21 in 100 people who had tried cocaine were expected to become dependent at some point. The figures rest on people's own memories.

general.statement: Most Vietnam veterans who got over heroin addiction did it through treatment.
general.why: Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home, and those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.

general.statement: Most people who were ever dependent on cocaine were still dependent decades later.
general.why: In a US survey, half had recovered within about 4 years, though some stayed dependent for decades. Recovery here means not counting as dependent for a year, not quitting.

nicotine.statement: Of people who try them, a bigger share become dependent on tobacco than on cocaine.
nicotine.why: In one US survey, about 68 in 100 people who'd smoked a full cigarette were expected to become dependent, against 21 in 100 for cocaine. These are projections from people's memories.

heroin.statement: Most US soldiers addicted to heroin in Vietnam stayed addicted after coming home.
heroin.why: Of the men addicted in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years. Vietnam's conditions were unusual.

cocaine.statement: People got over cocaine and cannabis dependence faster than alcohol or cigarette dependence.
cocaine.why: In a US survey, half had recovered within about 4 years for cocaine and 6 for cannabis, against 16 for alcohol and 30 for cigarettes. Recovery here means not counting as dependent for a year, not quitting.
